title: V3-9 — Climate & Materials Science: How the Bahamas Attacks Buildings

concepts.title: How the Bahamas attacks a building
concepts.mechanism: This climate's attack on a building is constant and chemical rather than sudden and violent — outside of hurricanes, it's salt aerosol soaking steadily into everything, humidity condensing on cool surfaces, UV breaking down exposed materials, and biological growth in the damp warmth. Knowing your enemy list matters as much as knowing what's NOT on it: freeze-thaw cycling, frost heave, and snow load simply do not happen here, and specifying for them wastes real money on protection this building will never need. Climate sets the baseline spec; day-to-day weather (a storm, a heat wave) is what decides whether today's work can proceed.
concepts.mechanismPro: Exposure classification drives cover, coatings, and material selection for chloride/UV/humidity resistance; explicitly de-scope freeze-thaw and frost-depth provisions common in temperate-climate specs — copying a mainland spec wholesale over-engineers for enemies that don't exist here and may under-engineer for the ones that do.
concepts.hook: Packing a parka and snow boots for a trip to a tropical island wastes suitcase space you needed for sunscreen and rain gear — the wrong enemy list costs you twice: once in what you didn't need, once in what you forgot.

applied.prompt: A structural spec drafted from a mainland US template includes frost-depth footing requirements and no explicit chloride-exposure cover upgrade for coastal elements. Your call?

options.label: Strip the frost-depth provisions and add proper chloride-exposure cover/mix requirements for the coastal condition
options.outcome: Right. This redirects spec budget from an enemy that isn't here to the one that actually attacks every marine-exposed structure on this project.

options.label: Leave the frost provisions in as harmless extra margin and separately add chloride cover
options.outcome: Adds the needed protection but wastes money on frost provisions that do nothing here — defensible only as a low-priority cleanup, not the ideal use of budget.

options.label: Use the template spec as-is since it's a recognized standard
options.outcome: A 'recognized' standard for the wrong climate is not free — it spends money protecting against frost that will never occur while leaving the real, constant chloride attack under-addressed.

applied.debrief: This is S9's chloride-ingress law at the scale of the whole climate: cover and dense concrete are the answer wherever salt is the enemy, whether that's a single marina structure in S9 or every coastal element project-wide here. Knowing your climate's specific enemy list — and its NOT-enemies — is where real specification money gets saved or wasted.

summary: Tropical-marine means the attack is constant, chemical, and biological rather than violent (except hurricanes): salt aerosol, humidity + dew point, UV, biology — and knowing what you DON'T face (freeze-thaw, frost depth, snow) is real money. Plus weather-vs-climate on the jobsite: climate sets your specs; weather sets your day. PLAIN: know your enemy list, and your not-enemy list. PRO: exposure classes, dew-point discipline, the vapor-barrier flip, weather task gating.

sections.heading: Your climate's weapons, ranked
sections.body: PLAIN: (1) SALT AEROSOL — the sea throws microscopic salt into the air; it settles on everything within roughly a mile of shore, worst in the first few hundred feet (your beach club and condos 1–2 are in the kill zone). Salt + metal + moisture = a corrosion battery running 24/7, attacking ABOVE ground: condensers, panels, hardware, fixtures. (2) HUMIDITY + HEAT — the engine for everything else: corrosion roughly doubles pace per ~18°F where moisture's present; mold farms any surface sustained above ~60–70% RH; and DEW POINT is the sneaky mechanism — chill any surface below the air's dew point (here 72–75°F much of the year) and water condenses on it out of thin air. Every over-cooled wall, every uninsulated chilled pipe, every duct in a hot attic is a condensation machine. This is WHY oversized AC = mold (S7). (3) UV — tropical sun is a slow flamethrower for polymers: paints chalk, sealants embrittle; budget repaint/reseal at roughly half temperate intervals (5–8 yr exposed coastal). (4) BIOLOGY — mold, subterranean and drywood termites (another reason for the concrete culture), marine borers, roots in every joint. (5) HURRICANES — the violent exception; the materials angle is WIND-DRIVEN RAIN: water arriving horizontally under pressure, testing flashings and window installs at pressures gravity never applies. PRO: 'C5-marine coating environment,' 'coastal-rated everything within the kill zone,' 'keep surfaces above dew point,' 'water-managed wall assembly, glazing tested at design pressure.'

sections.heading: What you DON'T face, and the comparative table
sections.body: PLAIN: No freeze-thaw (so no air-entrainment in concrete), no frost depth (footings can sit nearly at grade on rock — northern builders dig 4 ft purely to get below frost), no snow load, minimal seismic, small daily temperature swings. Knowing what NOT to pay for is real money — the sim includes 'delete the irrelevant spec item' problems. The comparative literacy: COLD/WET fights freeze-thaw, frost heave, snow, interior vapor barriers, road-salt corrosion. HOT-ARID fights giant daily swings (double the joint math), flash-drying, dust, expansive clays (heave — settlement in reverse). TEMPERATE fights long damp, rot, moss. TROPICAL-MARINE (you) fights chemistry and biology over ice and physics. The professional's transfer skill: arrive anywhere, ask 'which enemy dominates here,' re-rank every spec decision accordingly. PRO: exposure/durability classes by code region — F freeze-thaw, C chlorides (yours), S sulfates; the vapor-barrier flip (V3-5) as the interview classic.

sections.heading: Weather (days) vs climate (years) on the jobsite
sections.body: PLAIN: Climate sets your specs; weather sets your day. RAIN: no concrete finishing (ruined surface), no compacting wet fill (pumping), no painting/render, no asphalt on wet base, trench safety review. HEAT: concrete evaporation-rate limits (the S2 kit), worker heat-stress productivity drops measurably on peak afternoons (10–30%) — hydration, shade, and schedule shifts are safety AND productivity; asphalt actually LIKES heat (longer compaction window). WIND: crane lifts stop around 20–30 mph, plastic-shrinkage risk multiplies, no membrane/sheet work, dust complaints. STORM WATCH: the 72/48/24-hour preparedness ladder. PRO: the app's weather engine gates tasks exactly this way — weather state → blocked/degraded tasks → productivity multipliers — so the player internalizes which trades die on which forecast.

quiz.teach: The sweating-glass analogy: a cold drink sweats because its surface is below the air's dew point.
quiz.prompt: Why does an over-cooled condo wall grow mold in this climate?

choices.text: The chilled surface drops below the humid air's dew point (72–75°F here much of the year) and condenses water out of thin air — sustained surface moisture above the ~60–70% RH threshold is a mold farm; walls sweat exactly like the cold glass
choices.why: Correct. Indoor rain by refrigeration: the wall didn't leak — it CONDENSED. Keep surfaces above dew point (right-sized AC, insulated chilled surfaces, ducts in conditioned space) and the farm never opens.
Spores are everywhere always — the limiting resource is WATER, and the cold surface manufactures it from humid air.

choices.text: The AC's condensate drains leak into the wall
choices.why: A real but separate defect. The dew-point mechanism needs no leak — the moisture arrives through the air, invisibly, nightly.

choices.text: Paint in the tropics traps moisture
choices.why: Coating permeability matters at the margins; the driver is surface temperature vs dew point. Fix the temperature and the paint is irrelevant.

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: chill anything below the air's sweat-line and it drips — walls included. PRO: 'keep surfaces above dew point; vapor drive runs outside-in here; mold is a design defect wearing a housekeeping costume.' (V3-9, S7, V3-5)

quiz.teach: Knowing what NOT to pay for is climate literacy's cash value.
quiz.prompt: Which spec item should be DELETED from a set adapted from Florida/US-northern standards?

choices.text: Air-entrainment in the concrete and 4-ft frost-depth footings — both are armor against freeze-thaw and frost heave, enemies that never visit this island; footings on rock can found nearly at grade
choices.why: Correct. Air-entrainment costs strength and money to defeat ice that never forms; frost-depth digging is pure imported habit. Delete both, spend the savings on the chloride war you ARE fighting.

choices.text: The impact glazing — it's a cold-climate item
choices.why: Backwards — impact protection is a HURRICANE item and non-negotiable here (S6's internal pressurization). Know which armor is yours.
That's your PRIMARY enemy's armor (chlorides, S9) — the last thing to delete.

choices.text: Nothing — more protection is always safer
choices.why: Irrelevant protection isn't safe, it's expensive — and sometimes harmful (air-entrainment trades away strength; interior vapor barriers actively damage tropical walls).

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: don't buy a snow shovel for Nassau — and notice the specs that ARE snow shovels. PRO: 'exposure class C governs here, not F; delete freeze-thaw provisions, keep every chloride and wind provision, and flag any detail imported from a different climate for review.' (V3-9, V3-5)

quiz.teach: The weather engine's task-gating table: which trades die on which forecast.
quiz.prompt: Tomorrow's forecast: 25–30 mph sustained wind, dry, hot. Which activities are blocked or degraded?

choices.text: Crane lifts stop (20–30 mph limits), membrane/sheet work is off, and any concrete finishing carries multiplied plastic-shrinkage risk (wind is the evaporation-rate driver) — while earthwork and interior trades run normally, and asphalt actually benefits from the heat
choices.why: Correct. Wind is the crane-killer and the slab-surface killer; heat alone extends the asphalt window. Reading the forecast BY TRADE is the daily scheduling skill.

choices.text: Everything stops — high wind is high wind
choices.why: Blanket shutdowns waste the trades wind doesn't touch. The skill is selective gating: the excavator doesn't care; the crane and the fresh slab do.
Rain is one column of the table, not the whole table. Dry 28-mph wind grounds every crane pick and shreds every unweighted membrane on site.
Marine work has the WINDOW (seasonal); land work has the DAY (task gating). Both calendars run simultaneously.

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: wind grounds cranes and dries fresh concrete too fast; heat helps asphalt; rain kills finishing and compaction — every forecast is a to-do list edit. PRO: 'weather state → blocked/degraded tasks → productivity multipliers,' the lookup the sim's weather engine runs. (V3-9)

quiz.teach: Wind-driven rain arrives horizontally, under pressure.
quiz.prompt: Why do wall assemblies that shed ordinary rain perfectly still leak in a tropical storm?

choices.text: Storm rain arrives horizontally under wind pressure — it climbs laps, penetrates joints, and pressurizes cavities that gravity-rain never tests; flashings, window installs, and drainage planes must be designed and TESTED at design pressure
choices.why: Correct. Gravity detailing assumes water falls down; a design storm throws it sideways and pushes. 'Test the glazing at design pressure' exists because the difference is qualitative.

choices.text: Storm rain is heavier per drop
choices.why: Volume matters less than VECTOR and PRESSURE — sideways water under load finds paths downward water never visits.

choices.text: They don't — code assemblies handle all rain
choices.why: Code assemblies handle what they're detailed and tested for; wind-driven-rain performance is a specific, testable property that generic details lack.

choices.text: Storm damage lets the water in first
choices.why: Intact assemblies leak under driven rain too — no breakage required, just pressure differentials across imperfect laps.

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: storms throw water sideways and push it uphill — walls built only for falling water lose. PRO: 'wind-driven rain intrusion; water-managed assembly; field-test glazing and flashings at design pressure before the season proves them for you.' (V3-9, S6)

mathProblems.context: Peak-summer afternoons cost 10–30% of output where work continues without schedule shifts. Price the tax on a month of summer labor — then compare to the cost of dawn starts.

decisionPoints.title: The tiered VE answer
decisionPoints.scenario: A value-engineering pass proposes a standard-duty hardware and fixtures package saving $340K across the program versus coastal-rated. The VE consultant's spreadsheet treats every building identically — but your buildings aren't identical: the beach club and condos 1–2 sit in the first few hundred feet of salt kill zone; the inland production houses sit a half-mile back behind vegetation.

options.label: Tier the spec by exposure zone: marine-grade in the kill zone (where the corrosion clock runs fastest), standard-duty inland where the aerosol load is a fraction — capturing most of the saving without buying the year-6 replacement wave on the flagship buildings
options.outcome: The tiered answer is the climate-literate one: exposure is a gradient, not a constant, and the spec should follow it. You keep perhaps 60% of the VE saving and none of the beach club's year-6 hardware failure — the correct VE answer was never all-or-nothing.

options.label: Take the full $340K — warranties exist
options.outcome: Inland, you'll get away with it; in the kill zone, salt does what salt does and warranties don't cover environment. The oceanfront replacement wave lands at year 5–7 in occupied buildings — the HOA sentiment event the sim's Phase 7 has been waiting for.

options.label: Refuse — marine-grade everywhere, no exceptions
options.outcome: Safe and wasteful: the inland houses' door hardware doesn't live in the aerosol zone, and the premium there buys protection against an enemy that barely visits. Blanket specs are the same climate illiteracy as blanket deletions, pointed the other way.

decisionPoints.debrief: Exposure zoning is the master move of climate-literate specification: rank the enemy's intensity across YOUR site (kill zone to sheltered inland), and let the spec tier follow the gradient. Most VE fights dissolve when 'where' enters the spreadsheet. (V3-9, S7, S9)
